newsitem.title: INDIA: India cement firms hope for steps to spur demand.
newsitem.headline: India cement firms hope for steps to spur demand.

text.p: The Indian cement industry is hoping that this week's budget will not add to its woes against the backdrop of a slowdown in demand and lack of progress in infrastructure spending, manufacturers and analysts said.
"Cement demand was good in the first six months (of 1996/97, April to March)," Yeshwant Deosthale, vice president of Larsen & Toubro Ltd, a leading cement maker, told Reuters last week.
He said year-on-year demand growth fell to about 10 percent in the second half from 13.0 percent in the first half.
A Reuters poll of producers last week showed the cement industry was looking forward to incentives in the budget to spur demand and profitability.
It wants abolition of the 20 percent import duty on coal, exemption of excise duties on cement used in concrete linings to save water and also for cement used to make concrete roads.
The industry would also like a reduction on import duty on cement project imports, bringing it on par with import of equipment for power projects, industry officials said.

Other suggestions, the poll found, include retaining the current specific rate of excise duty on cement (as against ad valorem duty on some other commodities) and repeal of the minimum alternate tax on companies imposed in the last budget.
"If infrastructure projects take off following (expected) budget incentives, it will help us," said a cement producer.
The cement industry is one of the biggest contributors to government revenues, paying about 18 billion rupees ($502 million) a year in various taxes.
Some analysts expect import duty on coal to be reduced to 10 percent, but said other fiscal reliefs seemed most unlikely.
"Given the government's funding problems, a reduction in the tax burden would be unlikely," said an equities analyst.

There is near unanimity that the railway budget, to be presented to parliament ahead of the federal budget, would raise freight rates, thereby raising cost of production and cost of cement to consumers, analysts said.
A proposed hike in petroleum product prices, delayed because of a political fallout, will also raise cement units' cost of production whenever it is implemented, analysts said.
Cement prices have been under pressure in recent months.
"Right now there is some seasonal pick-up in demand," said a cement analyst at a European brokerage in Bombay.
Analysts expect Indian cement demand in 1996/97 (April to March) to show 8.0 percent growth in contrast with 11.0 percent growth recorded in the previous year.
India produced 69 million tonnes of cement in 1995/96.
The Indian cement industry is the world's fourth-largest.
An official at a Bombay-based cement firm said prices were weakening in most markets except eastern and northern India.
He said it was significant that prices were trending downwards in western India, home to two of India's most industrialised states, Maharashtra and Gujarat.
Cement prices have fallen to 115-120 rupees per 50 kg bag in Gujarat from 140-150 rupees two months ago, he said.

"This is more because of a deceleration in the economy rather than oversupply," he said. Cement prices were showing signs of weakening in cement-deficit southern markets, where prices are traditionally the highest in the country, he said. ($1 = 35.88 rupees)
